html:
The Adal Sultanate was a Muslim state in the Horn of Africa, covering parts of what are now eastern Ethiopia, Djibouti and northern Somalia. The map shows it from 1492 to 1600. It grew out of the older sultanate of Ifat after the Ethiopian emperors crushed Ifat in the early 1400s, and its towns were Dakkar, then Harar from 1520, with the port of Zeila on the Gulf of Aden.

Adal and the Christian Ethiopian Empire fought for control of trade routes and highlands for over a century. The conflict peaked under the imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, called Gragn, "the left-handed":

  • In 1529 he defeated the emperor at Shimbra Kure.
  • Over the next decade his armies, with firearms obtained through Ottoman contacts, overran most of Ethiopia and burned many churches and monasteries.
  • Portugal sent about 400 musketeers to help Ethiopia in 1541.
  • Ahmad was killed in battle at Wayna Daga in 1543, and his conquests collapsed.

Both sides were exhausted, and the Oromo moved north into the lands between them. In 1577 the sultanate moved its capital from Harar to the Aussa oasis in the desert, and Adal faded away.
